Problem

Find the charge represented by 4,600 electrons.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 1 steps

  1. Count signed elementary charges

    Each electron carries negative charge.

    Q=Ne=4600(−1.602×10−19)=−7.3692×10−16 CQ=Ne=4600(-1.602\times10^{-19})=-7.3692\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm CQ=Ne=4600(−1.602×10−19)=−7.3692×10−16 C
Result
Q=−7.3692×10−16 CQ=-7.3692\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm CQ=−7.3692×10−16 C

Check. Negative charge is required for electrons.

Lecture examplePractice 1.1 · Proton chargeReviewed
Link to this problem

Problem

Find the charge represented by 10 billion protons.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Convert the count

    Ten billion is ten to the tenth.

    N=10×109=1010N=10\times10^9=10^{10}N=10×109=1010

  2. Multiply

    Each proton has positive elementary charge.

    Q=1010(1.602×10−19)=1.602×10−9 CQ=10^{10}(1.602\times10^{-19})=1.602\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm CQ=1010(1.602×10−19)=1.602×10−9 C
Result
Q=1.602 nCQ=1.602\ \mathrm{nC}Q=1.602 nC

Check. The last digit 1.6021 nC on the solution slide is a typographical inconsistency with its stated 1.602 constant.

Problem

Given q(t)=5t sin(4πt) mC, find i at t=0.5 s.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Differentiate using the product rule

    Current is the derivative of charge.

    i=5sin⁡(4πt)+20πtcos⁡(4πt) mAi=5\sin(4\pi t)+20\pi t\cos(4\pi t)\ \mathrm{mA}i=5sin(4πt)+20πtcos(4πt) mA

  2. Evaluate

    At half a second the sine is zero and cosine is one.

    i(0.5)=10π=31.416 mAi(0.5)=10\pi=31.416\ \mathrm{mA}i(0.5)=10π=31.416 mA
Result
i(0.5)=31.42 mAi(0.5)=31.42\ \mathrm{mA}i(0.5)=31.42 mA

Check. Units and signs follow the reference directions in the source diagram.

  1. Differentiate

    The constant contributes zero.

    i(t)=−15+30e−3t mAi(t)=-15+30e^{-3t}\ \mathrm{mA}i(t)=−15+30e−3t mA

  2. Evaluate

    Substitute one second.

    i(1)=−15+30e−3=−13.5064 mAi(1)=-15+30e^{-3}=-13.5064\ \mathrm{mA}i(1)=−15+30e−3=−13.5064 mA
Result
i(1)=−13.51 mAi(1)=-13.51\ \mathrm{mA}i(1)=−13.51 mA

Problem

For i(t)=(3t²−t) A, find charge entering between 1 and 2 seconds.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 1 steps

  1. Integrate over the requested interval

    Use net signed charge.

    Q=∫12(3t2−t)dt=[t3−t2/2]12=6−0.5Q=\int_1^2(3t^2-t)dt=[t^3-t^2/2]_1^2=6-0.5Q=∫12​(3t2−t)dt=[t3−t2/2]12​=6−0.5
Result
Q=5.5 CQ=5.5\ \mathrm CQ=5.5 C

Check. Units and signs follow the reference directions in the source diagram.

Problem

Current is 8 A for 0<t<1 s and 8t² A for t>1 s. Find charge from 0 to 2 s.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 1 steps

  1. Split at the change

    Integrate each expression only where it applies.

    Q=∫018dt+∫128t2dt=8+83(8−1)=803Q=\int_0^1 8dt+\int_1^2 8t^2dt=8+\frac83(8-1)=\frac{80}3Q=∫01​8dt+∫12​8t2dt=8+38​(8−1)=380​
Result
Q=26.67 CQ=26.67\ \mathrm CQ=26.67 C

Check. Units and signs follow the reference directions in the source diagram.

Problem

A bulb carries 2 A for 10 s and releases 2.3 kJ. Find its voltage drop.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Find transferred charge

    Constant current gives charge directly.

    Q=It=2(10)=20 CQ=It=2(10)=20\ \mathrm CQ=It=2(10)=20 C

  2. Divide energy by charge

    Convert kilojoules to joules.

    V=W/Q=2300/20=115 VV=W/Q=2300/20=115\ \mathrm VV=W/Q=2300/20=115 V
Result
V=115 VV=115\ \mathrm VV=115 V

Check. Units and signs follow the reference directions in the source diagram.

Problem

Moving charge from b to a takes 100 J. Find v_ab for (a) 5 C and (b) −10 C.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 1 steps

  1. Use signed charge

    Potential difference is work per charge.

    vab=W/q;va=100/5=20 V,vb=100/(−10)=−10 Vv_{ab}=W/q;\quad v_a=100/5=20\ \mathrm V,\quad v_b=100/(-10)=-10\ \mathrm Vvab​=W/q;va​=100/5=20 V,vb​=100/(−10)=−10 V
Result
(a) 20 V;(b) −10 V(a)\ 20\ \mathrm V;\quad(b)\ -10\ \mathrm V(a) 20 V;(b) −10 V

Check. Units and signs follow the reference directions in the source diagram.

Problem

Current i=5cos(60πt) A enters the positive terminal. Find power at 3 ms for (a) v=3i and (b) v=3di/dt.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Resistive relation

    Use p=vi with time in seconds.

    pa=3i2=75cos⁡2(60πt);pa(0.003)=53.47 Wp_a=3i^2=75\cos^2(60\pi t);\quad p_a(0.003)=53.47\ \mathrm Wpa​=3i2=75cos2(60πt);pa​(0.003)=53.47 W

  2. Derivative relation

    Differentiate before multiplying by current.

    v=−900πsin⁡(60πt);pb=−4500πsin⁡(60πt)cos⁡(60πt)v=-900\pi\sin(60\pi t);\quad p_b=-4500\pi\sin(60\pi t)\cos(60\pi t)v=−900πsin(60πt);pb​=−4500πsin(60πt)cos(60πt)

  3. Evaluate

    Use 60π(0.003)=0.18π.

    pb(0.003)=−6395.85 Wp_b(0.003)=-6395.85\ \mathrm Wpb​(0.003)=−6395.85 W
Result
(a) 53.47 W;(b) −6.396 kW(a)\ 53.47\ \mathrm W;\quad(b)\ -6.396\ \mathrm{kW}(a) 53.47 W;(b) −6.396 kW

Check. Negative instantaneous absorbed power means energy is being supplied at that instant.

Problem

For i=5cos(60πt) A, find power at 5 ms for (a) v=6i and (b) v=6+10∫₀ᵗi(τ)dτ V.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Part a

    Evaluate the squared current.

    pa=150cos⁡2(0.3π)=51.824 Wp_a=150\cos^2(0.3\pi)=51.824\ \mathrm Wpa​=150cos2(0.3π)=51.824 W

  2. Part b voltage

    Integrate the current from zero.

    v=6+1012πsin⁡(60πt);v(0.005)=6.21460 Vv=6+\frac{10}{12\pi}\sin(60\pi t);\quad v(0.005)=6.21460\ \mathrm Vv=6+12π10​sin(60πt);v(0.005)=6.21460 V

  3. Part b power

    Multiply by the simultaneous current.

    i(0.005)=2.93893 A;pb=6.21460(2.93893)=18.2643 Wi(0.005)=2.93893\ \mathrm A;\quad p_b=6.21460(2.93893)=18.2643\ \mathrm Wi(0.005)=2.93893 A;pb​=6.21460(2.93893)=18.2643 W
Result
(a) 51.82 W;(b) 18.26 W(a)\ 51.82\ \mathrm W;\quad(b)\ 18.26\ \mathrm W(a) 51.82 W;(b) 18.26 W

Check. Units and signs follow the reference directions in the source diagram.

  2. Find energy

Problem

Calculate power supplied or absorbed by each element in the pictured circuit: I=5 A, branch current 6 A, and dependent current 0.2I.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Apply the passive sign convention

    P1 and P4 currents enter their negative voltage terminals.

    P1=−20(5)=−100 W;P2=12(5)=60 WP_1=-20(5)=-100\ \mathrm W;\quad P_2=12(5)=60\ \mathrm WP1​=−20(5)=−100 W;P2​=12(5)=60 W

  2. Evaluate the remaining elements

    The dependent current equals 1 A.

    P3=8(6)=48 W;P4=−8(0.2×5)=−8 WP_3=8(6)=48\ \mathrm W;\quad P_4=-8(0.2\times5)=-8\ \mathrm WP3​=8(6)=48 W;P4​=−8(0.2×5)=−8 W
Result
(P1,P2,P3,P4)=(−100,60,48,−8) W(P_1,P_2,P_3,P_4)=(-100,60,48,-8)\ \mathrm W(P1​,P2​,P3​,P4​)=(−100,60,48,−8) W

Check. Power balance: −100+60+48−8=0 W.

Link to this problem

Problem

The plotted charge rises 0→30 mC over 0–2 ms, stays constant to 8 ms, and falls to zero at 12 ms. Find current at 2, 6, and 8 ms and sketch i(t).

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Calculate slopes

    mC divided by ms equals amperes, not milliamperes.

    i(t)={15 A0<t<2 ms02<t<8 ms−7.5 A8<t<12 msi(t)=\begin{cases}15\ \mathrm A&0<t<2\ \mathrm{ms}\\0&2<t<8\ \mathrm{ms}\\-7.5\ \mathrm A&8<t<12\ \mathrm{ms}\end{cases}i(t)=⎩⎨⎧​15 A0−7.5 A​0<t<2 ms2<t<8 ms8<t<12 ms​

  2. Handle corners explicitly

    At 2 ms the one-sided currents are 15 and 0 A; at 8 ms they are 0 and −7.5 A. The derivative has no unique value at either corner.

    i(6 ms)=0;i(2−)=15, i(2+)=0, i(8−)=0, i(8+)=−7.5 Ai(6\ \mathrm{ms})=0;\quad i(2^-)=15,\ i(2^+)=0,\ i(8^-)=0,\ i(8^+)=-7.5\ \mathrm Ai(6 ms)=0;i(2−)=15, i(2+)=0, i(8−)=0, i(8+)=−7.5 A
Result
i(6 ms)=0;i(2 ms),i(8 ms) undefined at ideal cornersi(6\ \mathrm{ms})=0;\quad i(2\ \mathrm{ms}),i(8\ \mathrm{ms})\text{ undefined at ideal corners}i(6 ms)=0;i(2 ms),i(8 ms) undefined at ideal corners

Check. Correction to instructor solution p.43: slopes are A, not mA; the corner times require one-sided values. Areas give 30−30=0 mC net charge.

Problem

Current rises linearly from 0 to 12 mA over 0–1 ms, then is 6 mA over 1–2 ms. Find total charge.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Triangle

    The first interval contributes triangular area.

    Q1=12(1 ms)(12 mA)=6 μCQ_1=\tfrac12(1\ \mathrm{ms})(12\ \mathrm{mA})=6\ \mu\mathrm CQ1​=21​(1 ms)(12 mA)=6 μC

  2. Rectangle

    Add the constant-current interval.

    Q2=(1 ms)(6 mA)=6 μC;Q=12 μCQ_2=(1\ \mathrm{ms})(6\ \mathrm{mA})=6\ \mu\mathrm C;\quad Q=12\ \mu\mathrm CQ2​=(1 ms)(6 mA)=6 μC;Q=12 μC
Result
Q=12 μCQ=12\ \mu\mathrm CQ=12 μC

Check. mA·ms equals μC.

Problem

Find i(t) for q(t): (a) (3t+8) mC; (b) (8t²+4t−2) C; (c) (3e⁻ᵗ−5e⁻²ᵗ) nC; (d) 10sin(120πt) pC; (e) 20e⁻⁴ᵗcos(50t) μC.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Polynomial derivatives

    Differentiate q with respect to seconds.

    ia=3 mA;ib=(16t+4) Ai_a=3\ \mathrm{mA};\quad i_b=(16t+4)\ \mathrm Aia​=3 mA;ib​=(16t+4) A

  2. Chain rule

    Differentiate the exponentials and sine.

    ic=(−3e−t+10e−2t) nA;id=1200πcos⁡(120πt) pAi_c=(-3e^{-t}+10e^{-2t})\ \mathrm{nA};\quad i_d=1200\pi\cos(120\pi t)\ \mathrm{pA}ic​=(−3e−t+10e−2t) nA;id​=1200πcos(120πt) pA

  3. Product rule

    Both the exponential and cosine vary.

    ie=−20e−4t[4cos⁡(50t)+50sin⁡(50t)] μAi_e=-20e^{-4t}[4\cos(50t)+50\sin(50t)]\ \mu\mathrm Aie​=−20e−4t[4cos(50t)+50sin(50t)] μA
Result
ia=3mA, ib=(16t+4)A, ic=(−3e−t+10e−2t)nA, id=1200πcos⁡(120πt)pA, ie=−20e−4t(4cos⁡50t+50sin⁡50t)μAi_a=3\mathrm{mA},\ i_b=(16t+4)\mathrm A,\ i_c=(-3e^{-t}+10e^{-2t})\mathrm{nA},\ i_d=1200\pi\cos(120\pi t)\mathrm{pA},\ i_e=-20e^{-4t}(4\cos50t+50\sin50t)\mu\mathrm Aia​=3mA, ib​=(16t+4)A, ic​=(−3e−t+10e−2t)nA, id​=1200πcos(120πt)pA, ie​=−20e−4t(4cos50t+50sin50t)μA

Check. Units and signs follow the reference directions in the source diagram.

Problem setProblem set 1 · Question 3Reviewed
Link to this problem

Problem

Find q(t): (a) i=3 A, q(0)=1 C; (b) i=(2t+5) mA, q(0)=0; (c) i=20cos(10t+π/6) μA, q(0)=2 μC.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Include initial charge

    Integrate from zero to t.

    q(t)=q(0)+∫0ti(τ)dτq(t)=q(0)+\int_0^t i(\tau)d\tauq(t)=q(0)+∫0t​i(τ)dτ

  2. Parts a and b

    Integrate the constant and polynomial.

    qa=(1+3t) C;qb=(t2+5t) mCq_a=(1+3t)\ \mathrm C;\quad q_b=(t^2+5t)\ \mathrm{mC}qa​=(1+3t) C;qb​=(t2+5t) mC

  3. Part c

    Subtract the sine at the lower limit.

    qc=2+2[sin⁡(10t+π/6)−sin⁡(π/6)]=1+2sin⁡(10t+π/6) μCq_c=2+2[\sin(10t+\pi/6)-\sin(\pi/6)]=1+2\sin(10t+\pi/6)\ \mu\mathrm Cqc​=2+2[sin(10t+π/6)−sin(π/6)]=1+2sin(10t+π/6) μC
Result
qa=(1+3t)C;qb=(t2+5t)mC;qc=[1+2sin⁡(10t+π/6)]μCq_a=(1+3t)\mathrm C;\quad q_b=(t^2+5t)\mathrm{mC};\quad q_c=[1+2\sin(10t+\pi/6)]\mu\mathrm Cqa​=(1+3t)C;qb​=(t2+5t)mC;qc​=[1+2sin(10t+π/6)]μC

Check. At t=0 these give the three specified initial charges. Correction: the instructor DOCX writes +2 μC as the integration constant in part (c); that would give q(0)=3 μC. The correct constant is +1 μC.

Problem

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Read the local slope

    Current equals charge slope.

    i(1ms)=30/2=15 A;i(6ms)=0i(1\mathrm{ms})=30/2=15\ \mathrm A;\quad i(6\mathrm{ms})=0i(1ms)=30/2=15 A;i(6ms)=0

  2. Falling segment

    Its slope is negative.

    i(10ms)=(0−30)/(12−8)=−7.5 Ai(10\mathrm{ms})=(0-30)/(12-8)=-7.5\ \mathrm Ai(10ms)=(0−30)/(12−8)=−7.5 A
Result
(15,0,−7.5) A(15,0,-7.5)\ \mathrm A(15,0,−7.5) A

Check. mC/ms = A. The requested times lie inside straight segments.

Problem

Current i(t)=6e⁻²ᵗ mA enters the positive terminal and v(t)=10di/dt V. Find charge from 0–2 s, absorbed power, and absorbed energy from 0–3 s.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Convert current to amperes

    The voltage relation uses the SI derivative.

    i=0.006e−2t;v=10(−0.012e−2t)=−0.12e−2t Vi=0.006e^{-2t};\quad v=10(-0.012e^{-2t})=-0.12e^{-2t}\ \mathrm Vi=0.006e−2t;v=10(−0.012e−2t)=−0.12e−2t V

  2. Charge and power

    Integrate current; multiply voltage and current.

    Q=0.003(1−e−4)=2.94505 mC;p=−0.00072e−4t WQ=0.003(1-e^{-4})=2.94505\ \mathrm{mC};\quad p=-0.00072e^{-4t}\ \mathrm WQ=0.003(1−e−4)=2.94505 mC;p=−0.00072e−4t W

  3. Energy

    Integrate signed power.

    W=∫03−0.00072e−4tdt=−0.00018(1−e−12) JW=\int_0^3-0.00072e^{-4t}dt=-0.00018(1-e^{-12})\ \mathrm JW=∫03​−0.00072e−4tdt=−0.00018(1−e−12) J
Result
Q=2.945 mC; p=−0.72e−4t mW; W=−0.1800 mJQ=2.945\ \mathrm{mC};\ p=-0.72e^{-4t}\ \mathrm{mW};\ W=-0.1800\ \mathrm{mJ}Q=2.945 mC; p=−0.72e−4t mW; W=−0.1800 mJ

Check. Negative absorbed energy indicates net delivery. Treating the numerical mA value as amperes would introduce a factor-of-1000 error in voltage.

Problem

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Ohm’s law and reciprocal resistance

    Use SI current.

    v=0.003(10000)=30 V;G=1/10000=100 μSv=0.003(10000)=30\ \mathrm V;\quad G=1/10000=100\ \mu\mathrm Sv=0.003(10000)=30 V;G=1/10000=100 μS

  2. Power

    The resistor absorbs energy.

    p=0.0032(10000)=0.09 Wp=0.003^2(10000)=0.09\ \mathrm Wp=0.0032(10000)=0.09 W
Result
v=30V,G=100μS,p=90mWv=30\mathrm V,\quad G=100\mu\mathrm S,\quad p=90\mathrm{mW}v=30V,G=100μS,p=90mW

  1. Current

    Divide the complete voltage waveform by R.

    i(t)=20sin⁡(πt)5000=4sin⁡(πt) mAi(t)=\frac{20\sin(\pi t)}{5000}=4\sin(\pi t)\ \mathrm{mA}i(t)=500020sin(πt)​=4sin(πt) mA

  2. Power

    Square the voltage and divide by resistance.

    p(t)=400sin⁡2(πt)5000=80sin⁡2(πt) mWp(t)=\frac{400\sin^2(\pi t)}{5000}=80\sin^2(\pi t)\ \mathrm{mW}p(t)=5000400sin2(πt)​=80sin2(πt) mW
Result
i=4sin⁡(πt)mA;p=80sin⁡2(πt)mWi=4\sin(\pi t)\mathrm{mA};\quad p=80\sin^2(\pi t)\mathrm{mW}i=4sin(πt)mA;p=80sin2(πt)mW

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Match the waveform coefficients

    Since p=v²/R, the cosine-squared terms cancel away from their zeros.

    R=152/0.030=7500 ΩR=15^2/0.030=7500\ \OmegaR=152/0.030=7500 Ω

  2. Find current

    The result extends continuously through the voltage zeros.

    i=15cos⁡(t)/7500=2cos⁡(t) mAi=15\cos(t)/7500=2\cos(t)\ \mathrm{mA}i=15cos(t)/7500=2cos(t) mA
Result
R=7.5 kΩ;i=2cos⁡(t)mAR=7.5\ \mathrm{k}\Omega;\quad i=2\cos(t)\mathrm{mA}R=7.5 kΩ;i=2cos(t)mA

b=4, n=3, ℓ=2b=4,\ n=3,\ \ell=2b=4, n=3, ℓ=2

Problem

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. First loop

    One 30 V source and one unknown voltage.

    −30+v=0 ⇒v=30 V-30+v=0\ \Rightarrow v=30\ \mathrm V−30+v=0 ⇒v=30 V

  2. Second loop

    The indicated v2 polarity is reversed relative to the loop drop.

    −20+v1−v2=0 ⇒v1−v2=20 V-20+v_1-v_2=0\ \Rightarrow v_1-v_2=20\ \mathrm V−20+v1​−v2​=0 ⇒v1​−v2​=20 V

  3. Third loop

    Both independent sources provide rises in the selected loop traversal.

    −10+v1−8−v2=0 ⇒v1−v2=18 V-10+v_1-8-v_2=0\ \Rightarrow v_1-v_2=18\ \mathrm V−10+v1​−8−v2​=0 ⇒v1​−v2​=18 V
Result
v=30V;v1−v2=20V (middle), 18V (right)v=30\mathrm V;\quad v_1-v_2=20\mathrm V\text{ (middle)},\ 18\mathrm V\text{ (right)}v=30V;v1​−v2​=20V (middle), 18V (right)

Check. The last two loops determine voltage differences; no resistance values are provided to determine each voltage separately.

    v1=2i=8 V;v2=−3i=−12 Vv_1=2i=8\ \mathrm V;\quad v_2=-3i=-12\ \mathrm Vv1​=2i=8 V;v2​=−3i=−12 V

v1=8V,v2=−12Vv_1=8\mathrm V,\quad v_2=-12\mathrm Vv1​=8V,v2​=−12V

Problem

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Write the control relation

    The bottom reference voltage opposes clockwise current.

    vo=−6iv_o=-6ivo​=−6i

  2. Apply KVL

    Use the drawn source polarities.

    −12+4i+2vo−4+6i=0-12+4i+2v_o-4+6i=0−12+4i+2vo​−4+6i=0

  3. Substitute and solve

    The dependent source changes the loop coefficient.

    −16+10i−12i=0;i=−8 A;vo=−6(−8)=48 V-16+10i-12i=0;\quad i=-8\ \mathrm A;\quad v_o=-6(-8)=48\ \mathrm V−16+10i−12i=0;i=−8 A;vo​=−6(−8)=48 V
Result
i=−8A,vo=48Vi=-8\mathrm A,\quad v_o=48\mathrm Vi=−8A,vo​=48V

Check. KVL check: −12−32+96−4−48=0 V.

Problem

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Equivalent resistance and voltage

    The 6 kΩ and 12 kΩ are in series.

    Req=9∥18=6 kΩ;vo=0.030(6000)=180 VR_{eq}=9\parallel18=6\ \mathrm{k}\Omega;\quad v_o=0.030(6000)=180\ \mathrm VReq​=9∥18=6 kΩ;vo​=0.030(6000)=180 V

  2. Branch currents

    Each branch sees 180 V.

    i9k=180/9000=20 mA;i6k=i12k=180/18000=10 mAi_{9k}=180/9000=20\ \mathrm{mA};\quad i_{6k}=i_{12k}=180/18000=10\ \mathrm{mA}i9k​=180/9000=20 mA;i6k​=i12k​=180/18000=10 mA

  3. Power

    The current source supplies the sum of resistor powers.

    Ps=180(0.030)=5.4 W;P9k=0.0202(9000)=3.6;P6k=0.0102(6000)=0.6;P12k=0.0102(12000)=1.2 WP_s=180(0.030)=5.4\ \mathrm W;\quad P_{9k}=0.020^2(9000)=3.6;\quad P_{6k}=0.010^2(6000)=0.6;\quad P_{12k}=0.010^2(12000)=1.2\ \mathrm WPs​=180(0.030)=5.4 W;P9k​=0.0202(9000)=3.6;P6k​=0.0102(6000)=0.6;P12k​=0.0102(12000)=1.2 W
Result
vo=180V; Ps=5.4W; (P9k,P6k,P12k)=(3.6,0.6,1.2)Wv_o=180\mathrm V;\ P_s=5.4\mathrm W;\ (P_{9k},P_{6k},P_{12k})=(3.6,0.6,1.2)\mathrm Wvo​=180V; Ps​=5.4W; (P9k​,P6k​,P12k​)=(3.6,0.6,1.2)W

Check. 3.6+0.6+1.2=5.4 W.

  2. Node B

    The 7 A entering splits into 2 A and i3.

    i3=7−2=5 Ai_3=7-2=5\ \mathrm Ai3​=7−2=5 A
Result
(i1,i2,i3)=(7,−1,5)A(i_1,i_2,i_3)=(7,-1,5)\mathrm A(i1​,i2​,i3​)=(7,−1,5)A

    Always nonnegative for positive resistance.

    PR=I2R=(−2)2(3)=12 WP_R=I^2R=(-2)^2(3)=12\ \mathrm WPR​=I2R=(−2)2(3)=12 W

  3. Source powers supplied

    Positive means delivered; negative means absorbed.

    P12=12I=−24 W;P10=−10I=20 W;P−8=(−8)I=16 WP_{12}=12I=-24\ \mathrm W;\quad P_{10}=-10I=20\ \mathrm W;\quad P_{-8}=(-8)I=16\ \mathrm WP12​=12I=−24 W;P10​=−10I=20 W;P−8​=(−8)I=16 W
Result

Problem

Find node voltages v1 and v2 in Fig. 3.3, taking the bottom conductor as ground.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Node 1

    The 5 A source enters node 1; express the two resistor currents as voltage differences.

    5=v1−v24+v12⇒3v1−v2=205=\frac{v_1-v_2}{4}+\frac{v_1}{2}\quad\Rightarrow\quad3v_1-v_2=205=4v1​−v2​​+2v1​​⇒3v1​−v2​=20

  2. Node 2

    Account for both current sources with their drawn directions.

    v1−v24+10=5+v26⇒−3v1+5v2=60\frac{v_1-v_2}{4}+10=5+\frac{v_2}{6}\quad\Rightarrow\quad-3v_1+5v_2=604v1​−v2​​+10=5+6v2​​⇒−3v1​+5v2​=60

  3. Eliminate and substitute

    Add the equations, then back-substitute.

    4v2=80;v2=20;v1=20+2034v_2=80;\quad v_2=20;\quad v_1=\frac{20+20}{3}4v2​=80;v2​=20;v1​=320+20​
Result
v1=13.333 V,v2=20 Vv_1=13.333\ \mathrm V,\quad v_2=20\ \mathrm Vv1​=13.333 V,v2​=20 V

Check. KCL at node 1: −1.667 + 6.667 = 5 A; both equations are satisfied.

Problem

Find node voltages v1 and v2 in Fig. 3.4.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Write KCL

    Use the bottom conductor as reference; the 12 A source leaves node 2.

    v12+v1−v26=3;v27+v2−v16=−12\frac{v_1}{2}+\frac{v_1-v_2}{6}=3;\quad\frac{v_2}{7}+\frac{v_2-v_1}{6}=-122v1​​+6v1​−v2​​=3;7v2​​+6v2​−v1​​=−12

  2. Clear denominators

    Solve the two equations together.

    4v1−v2=18;−7v1+13v2=−5044v_1-v_2=18;\quad-7v_1+13v_2=-5044v1​−v2​=18;−7v1​+13v2​=−504

  3. Substitute

    Insert v2 = 4v1 − 18 into the second equation.

    45v1=−270⇒v1=−6,v2=−4245v_1=-270\Rightarrow v_1=-6,\quad v_2=-4245v1​=−270⇒v1​=−6,v2​=−42
Result
v1=−6 V,v2=−42 Vv_1=-6\ \mathrm V,\quad v_2=-42\ \mathrm Vv1​=−6 V,v2​=−42 V

Check. Node 1: −3 + 6 = 3 A; node 2: −6 − 6 = −12 A.

Problem

Find all three node voltages in Fig. 3.5. The dependent current source is 2ix; ix flows rightward through 2 Ω.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Define the controlling current

    Keep the dependent source active.

    ix=(v1−v2)/2i_x=(v_1-v_2)/2ix​=(v1​−v2​)/2

  2. Write node equations

    Apply KCL at each of the three nonreference nodes.

    3v1−2v2−v3=12;−4v1+7v2−v3=0;2v1−3v2+v3=03v_1-2v_2-v_3=12;\quad-4v_1+7v_2-v_3=0;\quad2v_1-3v_2+v_3=03v1​−2v2​−v3​=12;−4v1​+7v2​−v3​=0;2v1​−3v2​+v3​=0

  3. Solve

    Adding the last two equations gives v1 = 2v2. Substitute into the remaining equations.

    v1=2v2;v3=−v2;5v2=12v_1=2v_2;\quad v_3=-v_2;\quad5v_2=12v1​=2v2​;v3​=−v2​;5v2​=12
Result
v1=4.8 V,v2=2.4 V,v3=−2.4 Vv_1=4.8\ \mathrm V,\quad v_2=2.4\ \mathrm V,\quad v_3=-2.4\ \mathrm Vv1​=4.8 V,v2​=2.4 V,v3​=−2.4 V

Check. ix = 1.2 A; node 1 supplies 1.8 + 1.2 = 3 A, and node 3 receives 1.8 + 0.6 = 2ix.

    The reference node is the bottom conductor.

    ix=v2/4i_x=v_2/4ix​=v2​/4

  2. Write KCL

    Retain the 4ix current source from node 3 toward node 2.

    5v1−2v2−3v3=24;4v1+5v2=0;−3v1+6v2+4v3=05v_1-2v_2-3v_3=24;\quad4v_1+5v_2=0;\quad-3v_1+6v_2+4v_3=05v1​−2v2​−3v3​=24;4v1​+5v2​=0;−3v1​+6v2​+4v3​=0

    v2=−0.8v1;v3=1.95v1;0.75v1=24v_2=-0.8v_1;\quad v_3=1.95v_1;\quad0.75v_1=24v2​=−0.8v1​;v3​=1.95v1​;0.75v1​=24
Result
v1=32 V,v2=−25.6 V,v3=62.4 Vv_1=32\ \mathrm V,\quad v_2=-25.6\ \mathrm V,\quad v_3=62.4\ \mathrm Vv1​=32 V,v2​=−25.6 V,v3​=62.4 V

Problem

Find branch currents I1, I2 and I3 in Fig. 3.18 using mesh analysis.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Left mesh

    Choose both mesh currents clockwise; the shared resistor carries i1 − i2.

    −15+5i1+10(i1−i2)+10=0⇒3i1−2i2=1-15+5i_1+10(i_1-i_2)+10=0\Rightarrow3i_1-2i_2=1−15+5i1​+10(i1​−i2​)+10=0⇒3i1​−2i2​=1

  2. Right mesh

    Include the 10 V source with the opposite traversal sign.

    6i2+4i2+10(i2−i1)−10=0⇒−i1+2i2=16i_2+4i_2+10(i_2-i_1)-10=0\Rightarrow-i_1+2i_2=16i2​+4i2​+10(i2​−i1​)−10=0⇒−i1​+2i2​=1

  3. Solve and map to branches

    Add the equations and use I3 = i1 − i2.

    i1=i2=1;I1=i1, I2=i2, I3=i1−i2i_1=i_2=1;\quad I_1=i_1,\ I_2=i_2,\ I_3=i_1-i_2i1​=i2​=1;I1​=i1​, I2​=i2​, I3​=i1​−i2​
Result
I1=1 A,I2=1 A,I3=0I_1=1\ \mathrm A,\quad I_2=1\ \mathrm A,\quad I_3=0I1​=1 A,I2​=1 A,I3​=0

Check. The middle node is 10 V from either path, so the middle 10 Ω resistor has zero voltage and current.

Result
Io=1.5 AI_o=1.5\ \mathrm AIo​=1.5 A

    The 6 A source flows from node 1 to node 2.

    −v110−v15=6+v1−v22⇒−8v1+5v2=60-\frac{v_1}{10}-\frac{v_1}{5}=6+\frac{v_1-v_2}{2}\Rightarrow-8v_1+5v_2=60−10v1​​−5v1​​=6+2v1​−v2​​⇒−8v1​+5v2​=60

  2. Node 2

    Include the 3 A source entering node 2.

    v24=3+6+v1−v22⇒−2v1+3v2=36\frac{v_2}{4}=3+6+\frac{v_1-v_2}{2}\Rightarrow-2v_1+3v_2=364v2​​=3+6+2v1​−v2​​⇒−2v1​+3v2​=36

  3. Solve

    Eliminate v1.

    7v2=84⇒v2=12,v1=07v_2=84\Rightarrow v_2=12,\quad v_1=07v2​=84⇒v2​=12,v1​=0
Result
v1=0 V,v2=12 Vv_1=0\ \mathrm V,\quad v_2=12\ \mathrm Vv1​=0 V,v2​=12 V

Check. At node 2 the 9 A source injection splits into 6 A toward node 1 and 3 A through 4 Ω.

  3. Apply Ohm’s law

    Use each branch resistance without changing the reference directions.

    i1=vo/10=−6; i2=vo/20=−3; i3=vo/30=−2; i4=vo/60=−1i_1=v_o/10=-6;\ i_2=v_o/20=-3;\ i_3=v_o/30=-2;\ i_4=v_o/60=-1i1​=vo​/10=−6; i2​=vo​/20=−3; i3​=vo​/30=−2; i4​=vo​/60=−1
Result
vo=−60 V;(i1,i2,i3,i4)=(−6,−3,−2,−1) Av_o=-60\ \mathrm V;\quad(i_1,i_2,i_3,i_4)=(-6,-3,-2,-1)\ \mathrm Avo​=−60 V;(i1​,i2​,i3​,i4​)=(−6,−3,−2,−1) A

Check. The resistor currents sum to −12 A and balance the net 12 A leaving in the source branches.

    The 6 A source and 3 A inter-node source both inject current into node 1.

  3. Branch currents

    Divide each node voltage by its branch resistance.

    i1=60/20=3; i2=60/10=6; i3=i4=−20/40=−0.5i_1=60/20=3;\ i_2=60/10=6;\ i_3=i_4=-20/40=-0.5i1​=60/20=3; i2​=60/10=6; i3​=i4​=−20/40=−0.5
Result
i1=3 A, i2=6 A, i3=i4=−0.5 Ai_1=3\ \mathrm A,\ i_2=6\ \mathrm A,\ i_3=i_4=-0.5\ \mathrm Ai1​=3 A, i2​=6 A, i3​=i4​=−0.5 A

Check. The two left currents total 9 A; the two right currents total −1 A, matching the respective source injections.

  2. 6 V contribution

    i2=−6/4=−1.5 Ai_2=-6/4=-1.5\ \mathrm Ai2​=−6/4=−1.5 A

  3. Add responses

    Superpose currents algebraically.

    i=i1+i2=2.5−1.5i=i_1+i_2=2.5-1.5i=i1​+i2​=2.5−1.5
Result
i=1 A clockwisei=1\ \mathrm A\ \text{clockwise}i=1 A clockwise

Transform the three pictured source-resistor pairs between voltage-source and current-source forms, preserving terminal polarity.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. 21 V and 3 Ω

    The positive upper terminal corresponds to an upward Norton current.

    IN=21/3=7 A;RN=3 ΩI_N=21/3=7\ \mathrm A;\quad R_N=3\ \OmegaIN​=21/3=7 A;RN​=3 Ω

  2. 40 V and 8 Ω

    The shown voltage polarity corresponds to a downward Norton current.

    ∣IN∣=40/8=5 A;RN=8 Ω|I_N|=40/8=5\ \mathrm A;\quad R_N=8\ \Omega∣IN​∣=40/8=5 A;RN​=8 Ω

  3. Dependent source

    The control variable remains unchanged by the transformation.

    IN=(8ix)/2=4ix;RN=2 ΩI_N=(8i_x)/2=4i_x;\quad R_N=2\ \OmegaIN​=(8ix​)/2=4ix​;RN​=2 Ω
Result
21V/3Ω↔7A∥3Ω;40V/8Ω↔5A∥8Ω;8ix/2Ω↔4ix∥2Ω21\mathrm V/3\Omega\leftrightarrow7\mathrm A\parallel3\Omega;\quad40\mathrm V/8\Omega\leftrightarrow5\mathrm A\parallel8\Omega;\quad8i_x/2\Omega\leftrightarrow4i_x\parallel2\Omega21V/3Ω↔7A∥3Ω;40V/8Ω↔5A∥8Ω;8ix​/2Ω↔4ix​∥2Ω

Check. For each pair, the open-circuit voltage is IsR and the short-circuit current is Vs/R; arrows and polarities follow the displayed diagrams.

Problem

Find v1 across the 6 Ω resistor fed by the 16 A source in parallel with 2 Ω.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Transform source

    Replace 16 A in parallel with 2 Ω by 32 V in series with 2 Ω.

    Vs=16(2)=32 VV_s=16(2)=32\ \mathrm VVs​=16(2)=32 V

  2. Find load current

    The transformed circuit is a series loop.

    i=32/(2+6)=4 Ai=32/(2+6)=4\ \mathrm Ai=32/(2+6)=4 A

  3. Find load voltage

    Multiply the load current by 6 Ω.

    v1=6(4)v_1=6(4)v1​=6(4)
Result
v1=24 Vv_1=24\ \mathrm Vv1​=24 V

Check. Original circuit: 24/2 + 24/6 = 12+4 = 16 A.

Problem

Use source transformation to find vo across 8 Ω in Fig. 4.17.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Transform the left source

    3 A downward in parallel with 4 Ω becomes 12 V with negative terminal at the top; its series resistance plus 2 Ω is 6 Ω.

    Rleft=4+2=6 Ω;Ileft=−12/6=−2 AR_{\mathrm{left}}=4+2=6\ \Omega;\quad I_{\mathrm{left}}=-12/6=-2\ \mathrm ARleft​=4+2=6 Ω;Ileft​=−12/6=−2 A

  2. Transform the right source

    12 V with 3 Ω becomes 4 A upward. Combine source currents and parallel resistances.

    Inet=4−2=2 A;6∥3=2 ΩI_{\mathrm{net}}=4-2=2\ \mathrm A;\quad6\parallel3=2\ \OmegaInet​=4−2=2 A;6∥3=2 Ω

  3. Find output

    The 2 A source feeds 8 Ω in parallel with 2 Ω.

    vo=2(8∥2)=21610v_o=2(8\parallel2)=2\frac{16}{10}vo​=2(8∥2)=21016​
Result
vo=3.2 Vv_o=3.2\ \mathrm Vvo​=3.2 V

Check. Original-node check: left node is −1.8667 V; output KCL is (3.2+1.8667)/2 + 3.2/8 + (3.2−12)/3 = 0.

Problem

Use source transformation to find vx in Fig. 4.20 with dependent current source 0.25vx.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Transform both source pairs

    6 V with 2 Ω becomes 3 A in parallel with 2 Ω. Combining that resistor with the vertical 2 Ω gives 1 Ω; this pair becomes 3 V in series with 1 Ω.

    2∥2=1 Ω;Vs=3(1)=3 V2\parallel2=1\ \Omega;\quad V_s=3(1)=3\ \mathrm V2∥2=1 Ω;Vs​=3(1)=3 V

  2. Transform the dependent source

    Its equivalent voltage is 4(0.25vx) = vx, positive on the left. Keep its control voltage referenced to the original output terminals.

    −vx+4i+vx+18=0⇒i=−4.5 A-v_x+4i+v_x+18=0\Rightarrow i=-4.5\ \mathrm A−vx​+4i+vx​+18=0⇒i=−4.5 A

  3. Find vx

    Apply KVL around the left portion.

    −3+i+vx=0⇒vx=3−(−4.5)-3+i+v_x=0\Rightarrow v_x=3-(-4.5)−3+i+vx​=0⇒vx​=3−(−4.5)
Result
vx=7.5 Vv_x=7.5\ \mathrm Vvx​=7.5 V

Check. Original KCL: (7.5−6)/2 + 7.5/2 + (7.5−18)/4 − 0.25(7.5) = 0.

Problem

Find the Thévenin equivalent seen by the 3.3 kΩ load, then its current and voltage. The source is 10 V; R1 = 3.9 kΩ, R2 = 4.7 kΩ, R3 = 8.2 kΩ.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Open the load

    No current flows through 4.7 kΩ; use the 3.9 kΩ–8.2 kΩ divider.

    VTh=108.23.9+8.2=6.77686 VV_{Th}=10\frac{8.2}{3.9+8.2}=6.77686\ \mathrm VVTh​=103.9+8.28.2​=6.77686 V

  2. Deactivate source

    Short the voltage source and look into the load terminals.

    RTh=4.7+(3.9∥8.2)=7.34298 kΩR_{Th}=4.7+(3.9\parallel8.2)=7.34298\ \mathrm{k\Omega}RTh​=4.7+(3.9∥8.2)=7.34298 kΩ

  3. Reconnect load

    Use series current and the load voltage drop.

    IL=6.776867.34298+3.3=0.636744 mA;VL=3.3IL=2.10125 VI_L=\frac{6.77686}{7.34298+3.3}=0.636744\ \mathrm{mA};\quad V_L=3.3I_L=2.10125\ \mathrm VIL​=7.34298+3.36.77686​=0.636744 mA;VL​=3.3IL​=2.10125 V
Result
VTh=6.777 V, RTh=7.343 kΩ; IL=0.6367 mA, VL=2.101 VV_{Th}=6.777\ \mathrm V,\ R_{Th}=7.343\ \mathrm{k\Omega};\ I_L=0.6367\ \mathrm{mA},\ V_L=2.101\ \mathrm VVTh​=6.777 V, RTh​=7.343 kΩ; IL​=0.6367 mA, VL​=2.101 V

Check. Direct reduction using 8.2 kΩ in parallel with (4.7+3.3) kΩ yields the same load current.

Problem

Find the Thévenin equivalent at a–b and the current through the 6 Ω load in the pictured 32 V circuit.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Open-circuit voltage

    Remove the 6 Ω load. The 12 Ω resistor sets the open-circuit divider voltage; any output series resistor has zero drop.

    VTh=32124+12=24 VV_{Th}=32\frac{12}{4+12}=24\ \mathrm VVTh​=324+1212​=24 V

  2. Equivalent resistance

    Short the 32 V source; combine 4 Ω and 12 Ω in parallel, then include any output series resistance.

    RTh=(4∥12)+0=3 ΩR_{Th}=(4\parallel12)+0=3\ \OmegaRTh​=(4∥12)+0=3 Ω

  3. Reconnect load

    Apply Ohm’s law to the equivalent series circuit.

    IL=24/(3+6)=8/3 AI_L=24/(3+6)=8/3\ \mathrm AIL​=24/(3+6)=8/3 A
Result
VTh=24 V, RTh=3 Ω, IL=8/3 AV_{Th}=24\ \mathrm V,\ R_{Th}=3\ \Omega,\ I_L=8/3\ \mathrm AVTh​=24 V, RTh​=3 Ω, IL​=8/3 A

Check. The source-off resistance and open-circuit voltage determine the same loaded terminal behavior as the original divider.

Problem

Find current and load power for a 20 V source with 10 Ω internal resistance and a 5 Ω load.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Total resistance

    Add internal and load resistances.

    RT=10+5=15 ΩR_T=10+5=15\ \OmegaRT​=10+5=15 Ω

  2. Current

    Apply Ohm’s law.

    I=20/15=1.33333 AI=20/15=1.33333\ \mathrm AI=20/15=1.33333 A

  3. Load power

    Use only the load resistance in I²R.

    PL=(20/15)2(5)=8.88889 WP_L=\left(20/15\right)^2(5)=8.88889\ \mathrm WPL​=(20/15)2(5)=8.88889 W
Result
I=1.33333 A, PL=8.88889 WI=1.33333\ \mathrm A,\ P_L=8.88889\ \mathrm WI=1.33333 A, PL​=8.88889 W

Check. Among 5 Ω, 10 Ω and 15 Ω, the 10 Ω load receives the most power because it matches the source resistance.

Problem

Find RL for maximum power transfer in Fig. 4.50 and calculate that maximum power.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Thévenin resistance

    Short 12 V and open 2 A.

    RTh=2+3+(6∥12)=9 ΩR_{Th}=2+3+(6\parallel12)=9\ \OmegaRTh​=2+3+(6∥12)=9 Ω

  2. Open-circuit voltage

    No current flows through the output 2 Ω resistor. At the current-source node V2 − V1 = 2(3) = 6 V.

    V1−126+V112=2⇒V1=16;VTh=V2=22\frac{V_1-12}{6}+\frac{V_1}{12}=2\Rightarrow V_1=16;\quad V_{Th}=V_2=226V1​−12​+12V1​​=2⇒V1​=16;VTh​=V2​=22

  3. Match the load

    For a resistive load, set RL equal to RTh.

    RL=9 Ω;Pmax=2224(9)=1219 WR_L=9\ \Omega;\quad P_{max}=\frac{22^2}{4(9)}=\frac{121}{9}\ \mathrm WRL​=9 Ω;Pmax​=4(9)222​=9121​ W
Result
RL=9 Ω,Pmax=13.444 WR_L=9\ \Omega,\quad P_{max}=13.444\ \mathrm WRL​=9 Ω,Pmax​=13.444 W

Check. At matching, load voltage is 11 V, so PL = 11²/9 = 13.444 W.

Problem

Use superposition to find rightward io and left-positive vo across 10 Ω in Fig. 4.79. Keep the dependent source 4io active.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. 6 A contribution

    Short the 30 V source. Let va and vb be the nodes on either side of 10 Ω; io1 = (va−vb)/10.

    va/40+io1=6;vb/20=5io1;va=vb+10io1⇒io1=1.6v_a/40+i_{o1}=6;\quad v_b/20=5i_{o1};\quad v_a=v_b+10i_{o1}\Rightarrow i_{o1}=1.6va​/40+io1​=6;vb​/20=5io1​;va​=vb​+10io1​⇒io1​=1.6

  2. 30 V contribution

    Open the 6 A source. The top of the 30 V source is −30 V.

    va/40+io2=0;(vb+30)/20=5io2;va−vb=10io2⇒io2=0.2v_a/40+i_{o2}=0;\quad(v_b+30)/20=5i_{o2};\quad v_a-v_b=10i_{o2}\Rightarrow i_{o2}=0.2va​/40+io2​=0;(vb​+30)/20=5io2​;va​−vb​=10io2​⇒io2​=0.2

  3. Add responses

    Retain the original current and voltage references.

    io=1.6+0.2=1.8 A;vo=10io=18 Vi_o=1.6+0.2=1.8\ \mathrm A;\quad v_o=10i_o=18\ \mathrm Vio​=1.6+0.2=1.8 A;vo​=10io​=18 V
Result
io=1.8 A,vo=18 Vi_o=1.8\ \mathrm A,\quad v_o=18\ \mathrm Vio​=1.8 A,vo​=18 V

Check. Full-circuit nodes are va = 168 V and vb = 150 V: 168/40+1.8 = 6 and (150+30)/20 = 5(1.8). The released key’s 17.99 V is premature rounding.

Problem

Use superposition to find left-positive vo across the 5 Ω resistor in Fig. 4.80.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 4 steps

  1. 2 A source alone

    Short both voltage sources. The alternate path is (6∥3)+(4∥12) = 5 Ω, equal to the output resistor.

    vo1=5(2/2)=5 Vv_{o1}=5(2/2)=5\ \mathrm Vvo1​=5(2/2)=5 V

  2. 12 V source alone

    Open 2 A and short 19 V. The right shunt becomes 3 Ω.

    Va=123∥86+(3∥8)=3.2;vo2=Va55+3=2V_a=12\frac{3\parallel8}{6+(3\parallel8)}=3.2;\quad v_{o2}=V_a\frac5{5+3}=2Va​=126+(3∥8)3∥8​=3.2;vo2​=Va​5+35​=2

  3. 19 V source alone

    Open 2 A and short 12 V. The left shunt becomes 2 Ω; the output polarity makes this contribution negative.

    Vb=1912∥74+(12∥7)=9.975;vo3=−57Vb=−7.125V_b=19\frac{12\parallel7}{4+(12\parallel7)}=9.975;\quad v_{o3}=-\frac57V_b=-7.125Vb​=194+(12∥7)12∥7​=9.975;vo3​=−75​Vb​=−7.125

  4. Sum

    Add all three signed responses.

    vo=5+2−7.125=−0.125 Vv_o=5+2-7.125=-0.125\ \mathrm Vvo​=5+2−7.125=−0.125 V
Result
vo=−125 mVv_o=-125\ \mathrm{mV}vo​=−125 mV

Check. Full-circuit nodal voltages are Va = 8.05 V and Vb = 8.175 V; their difference is −0.125 V.

Problem

Use superposition to find rightward io through 4 Ω in Fig. 4.84.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 4 steps

  1. 12 V source alone

    Open both current sources.

    Req=4+[10∥(3+2+5)]=9;io1=12/9R_{eq}=4+[10\parallel(3+2+5)]=9;\quad i_{o1}=12/9Req​=4+[10∥(3+2+5)]=9;io1​=12/9

  2. 4 A source alone

    Short 12 V and open 2 A. The alternate path across the 3 Ω source branch is 2+5+(4∥10) = 69/7 Ω.

    ialt=433+69/7=14/15;io2=−104+10ialt=−2/3i_{alt}=4\frac3{3+69/7}=14/15;\quad i_{o2}=-\frac{10}{4+10}i_{alt}=-2/3ialt​=43+69/73​=14/15;io2​=−4+1010​ialt​=−2/3

  3. 2 A source alone

    Short 12 V and open 4 A; the left route has resistance 3+2+(4∥10) = 55/7 Ω.

    ileft=255+55/7=7/9;io3=−101479=−5/9i_{left}=2\frac5{5+55/7}=7/9;\quad i_{o3}=-\frac{10}{14}\frac79=-5/9ileft​=25+55/75​=7/9;io3​=−1410​97​=−5/9

  4. Sum

    Negative contributions flow against the indicated rightward arrow.

    io=12/9−6/9−5/9=1/9i_o=12/9-6/9-5/9=1/9io​=12/9−6/9−5/9=1/9
Result
io=1/9 A=111.111 mAi_o=1/9\ \mathrm A=111.111\ \mathrm{mA}io​=1/9 A=111.111 mA

Check. Full-circuit node voltages after 4 Ω, after 3 Ω and at the right are 104/9 V, 121/45 V and 43/9 V. These satisfy KCL and io = (12−104/9)/4 = 1/9 A.

Problem

Find the Thévenin equivalent seen by the 5 Ω resistor in Fig. 4.101, then find its current.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Remove load

    With the load open, no current flows through the top 10 Ω resistor.

    VTh=4(10)=40 VV_{Th}=4(10)=40\ \mathrm VVTh​=4(10)=40 V

  2. Deactivate source

    Open 4 A; the two 10 Ω resistors are in series from the load terminals.

    RTh=10+10=20 ΩR_{Th}=10+10=20\ \OmegaRTh​=10+10=20 Ω

  3. Reconnect load

    Use the Thévenin series circuit.

    IL=40/(20+5)=1.6 AI_L=40/(20+5)=1.6\ \mathrm AIL​=40/(20+5)=1.6 A
Result
VTh=40 V, RTh=20 Ω, IL=1.6 AV_{Th}=40\ \mathrm V,\ R_{Th}=20\ \Omega,\ I_L=1.6\ \mathrm AVTh​=40 V, RTh​=20 Ω, IL​=1.6 A

Check. Independent short-circuit calculation gives Isc = 2 A, so Voc/Isc = 20 Ω.

Problem

Find the Norton equivalent at a–b of Fig. 4.104.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Resistance

    Short 120 V and open 2 A.

    RN=12∥(20+40)=10 ΩR_N=12\parallel(20+40)=10\ \OmegaRN​=12∥(20+40)=10 Ω

  2. Short-circuit current

    Short a–b, bypassing 12 Ω. Transform the 2 A/40 Ω pair into an opposing 80 V source.

    IN=Isc=120−2(40)20+40=23 AI_N=I_{sc}=\frac{120-2(40)}{20+40}=\frac23\ \mathrm AIN​=Isc​=20+40120−2(40)​=32​ A

  3. Specify equivalent

    Use a current source directed b to a in parallel with RN.

    Voc=INRN=203 VV_{oc}=I_NR_N=\frac{20}{3}\ \mathrm VVoc​=IN​RN​=320​ V
Result
IN=2/3 A,RN=10 ΩI_N=2/3\ \mathrm A,\quad R_N=10\ \OmegaIN​=2/3 A,RN​=10 Ω

Check. An independent open-circuit nodal solution gives Va = 20/3 V; division by RN recovers 2/3 A.

Problem

Use Thévenin’s theorem to find downward i through 40 Ω in Fig. 4.103.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Remove 40 Ω

    Apply KCL to the common top node.

    VTh−5010+VTh−3012=0⇒VTh=450/11 V\frac{V_{Th}-50}{10}+\frac{V_{Th}-30}{12}=0\Rightarrow V_{Th}=450/11\ \mathrm V10VTh​−50​+12VTh​−30​=0⇒VTh​=450/11 V

  2. Equivalent resistance

    Short both independent voltage sources.

    RTh=10∥12=60/11 ΩR_{Th}=10\parallel12=60/11\ \OmegaRTh​=10∥12=60/11 Ω

  3. Reconnect load

    Use the series equivalent.

    i=450/1140+60/11=0.9 Ai=\frac{450/11}{40+60/11}=0.9\ \mathrm Ai=40+60/11450/11​=0.9 A
Result
i=0.9 Ai=0.9\ \mathrm Ai=0.9 A

Check. Loaded voltage is 36 V; source branches inject (50−36)/10 + (30−36)/12 = 1.4−0.5 = 0.9 A.

Problem

Apply Thévenin’s theorem to find top-positive vo across the 10 Ω resistor in Fig. 4.105.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Equivalent resistance

    Remove 10 Ω, open 3 A and short 12 V.

    RTh=1+[5∥(4+16)]=5 ΩR_{Th}=1+[5\parallel(4+16)]=5\ \OmegaRTh​=1+[5∥(4+16)]=5 Ω

  2. Open-circuit voltage

    The 1 Ω output resistor has no current. Solve the left and middle node equations.

    5V1−4V2=48;−5V1+9V2=48⇒VTh=V2=19.2 V5V_1-4V_2=48;\quad-5V_1+9V_2=48\Rightarrow V_{Th}=V_2=19.2\ \mathrm V5V1​−4V2​=48;−5V1​+9V2​=48⇒VTh​=V2​=19.2 V

  3. Reconnect load

    Use the voltage divider.

    vo=19.2105+10=12.8 Vv_o=19.2\frac{10}{5+10}=12.8\ \mathrm Vvo​=19.25+1010​=12.8 V
Result
vo=12.8 Vv_o=12.8\ \mathrm Vvo​=12.8 V

Check. Load current is 1.28 A; Thévenin internal drop is 6.4 V, summing to 19.2 V.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Equivalent resistance

    Open 3 A and short 24 V.

    RTh=16+[5∥(10+10)]=20 ΩR_{Th}=16+[5\parallel(10+10)]=20\ \OmegaRTh​=16+[5∥(10+10)]=20 Ω

  2. Interior node voltages

    Let V1 be the upper-left node and V2 the middle node; 3 A flows through 16 Ω toward terminal a and returns through the source.

    2V1−V2=54;2V1−6V2=60⇒V2=−1.2 V2V_1-V_2=54;\quad2V_1-6V_2=60\Rightarrow V_2=-1.2\ \mathrm V2V1​−V2​=54;2V1​−6V2​=60⇒V2​=−1.2 V

  3. Terminal voltage

    Moving from V2 toward a gives a 48 V drop through 16 Ω.

    VTh=V2−3(16)=−49.2 VV_{Th}=V_2-3(16)=-49.2\ \mathrm VVTh​=V2​−3(16)=−49.2 V
Result
VTh=−49.2 V,RTh=20 ΩV_{Th}=-49.2\ \mathrm V,\quad R_{Th}=20\ \OmegaVTh​=−49.2 V,RTh​=20 Ω

Check. V1 = 26.4 V: (24−26.4)/10+3 = (26.4+1.2)/10 = 2.76 A. The key labels its resistance equation VThev once; units show it is RTh.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

    Open both current sources and short 14 V.

    RTh=RN=5∥(14+6)=4 ΩR_{Th}=R_N=5\parallel(14+6)=4\ \OmegaRTh​=RN​=5∥(14+6)=4 Ω

  2. Open-circuit voltage

    Transform 1 A with 6 Ω into 6 V in series with 6 Ω. This aids the 14 V source.

    6+14−VTh6+14=3+VTh5⇒VTh=−8 V\frac{6+14-V_{Th}}{6+14}=3+\frac{V_{Th}}5\Rightarrow V_{Th}=-8\ \mathrm V6+146+14−VTh​​=3+5VTh​​⇒VTh​=−8 V

  3. Norton current

    Define Isc positive from a to b, equivalently a Norton source positive from b to a.

    IN=VTh/RTh=−8/4=−2 AI_N=V_{Th}/R_{Th}=-8/4=-2\ \mathrm AIN​=VTh​/RTh​=−8/4=−2 A
Result
VTh=−8 V,RTh=RN=4 Ω,IN=−2 AV_{Th}=-8\ \mathrm V,\quad R_{Th}=R_N=4\ \Omega,\quad I_N=-2\ \mathrm AVTh​=−8 V,RTh​=RN​=4 Ω,IN​=−2 A

Worked solution · 3 steps

    Remove R; short both voltage sources and open 6 A.

    RTh=2∥(3+5)=1.6 ΩR_{Th}=2\parallel(3+5)=1.6\ \OmegaRTh​=2∥(3+5)=1.6 Ω

  2. Open-circuit voltage

    Transform the 6 A/5 Ω branch to a 30 V source with positive terminal at ground. Define counterclockwise loop current i.

    10i+20+10+30=0⇒i=−6 A;VTh+10+2i=0⇒VTh=2 V10i+20+10+30=0\Rightarrow i=-6\ \mathrm A;\quad V_{Th}+10+2i=0\Rightarrow V_{Th}=2\ \mathrm V10i+20+10+30=0⇒i=−6 A;VTh​+10+2i=0⇒VTh​=2 V

  3. Maximum-power condition

    Match the load to the positive Thévenin resistance.

    R=1.6 Ω;Pmax=VTh24RTh=46.4=0.625 WR=1.6\ \Omega;\quad P_{max}=\frac{V_{Th}^2}{4R_{Th}}=\frac4{6.4}=0.625\ \mathrm WR=1.6 Ω;Pmax​=4RTh​VTh2​​=6.44​=0.625 W
Result
R=1.6 Ω,Pmax=625 mWR=1.6\ \Omega,\quad P_{max}=625\ \mathrm{mW}R=1.6 Ω,Pmax​=625 mW

Check. At the match, load voltage is 1 V and current is 0.625 A, giving 0.625 W.

    q=(3×10−12)(20)=60 pCq=(3\times10^{-12})(20)=60\,\mathrm{pC}q=(3×10−12)(20)=60pC

  2. Energy

    Use the square of the voltage.

    w=12(3×10−12)(20)2=600 pJw=\tfrac12(3\times10^{-12})(20)^2=600\,\mathrm{pJ}w=21​(3×10−12)(20)2=600pJ
Result
q=60 pC,w=600 pJq=60\,\mathrm{pC},\quad w=600\,\mathrm{pJ}q=60pC,w=600pJ

    v(t)=6×10−32×10−6∫0te−3000s dsv(t)=\frac{6\times10^{-3}}{2\times10^{-6}}\int_0^t e^{-3000s}\,dsv(t)=2×10−66×10−3​∫0t​e−3000sds

  2. Evaluate bounds

    The exponential integral is (1 − e^{-3000t})/3000.

    v(t)=30003000(1−e−3000t)v(t)=\frac{3000}{3000}(1-e^{-3000t})v(t)=30003000​(1−e−3000t)
Result
v(t)=1−e−3000t Vv(t)=1-e^{-3000t}\,\mathrm Vv(t)=1−e−3000tV

  2. Calculate current

    Multiply each slope by 200 μF. Current is zero on constant-voltage sections.

    i=Cdvdt=(200×10−6)(±50)=±10 mAi=C\frac{dv}{dt}=(200\times10^{-6})(\pm50)=\pm10\,\mathrm{mA}i=Cdtdv​=(200×10−6)(±50)=±10mA
Result
i(t)={10 mA0<t<1−10 mA1<t<310 mA3<t<40otherwisei(t)=\begin{cases}10\,\mathrm{mA}&0<t<1\\-10\,\mathrm{mA}&1<t<3\\10\,\mathrm{mA}&3<t<4\\0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}i(t)=⎩⎨⎧​10mA−10mA10mA0​0<t<11<t<33<t<4otherwise​

Problem

An initially uncharged 1-mF capacitor carries a current rising linearly from 0 to 100 mA over 0–2 ms, then staying at 100 mA. Find voltage at 2 ms and 5 ms.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. First interval

    In seconds, i = 50t A. Integrate and divide by C = 0.001 F.

    v(t)=25000t2;v(0.002)=0.100 Vv(t)=25000t^2;\quad v(0.002)=0.100\,\mathrm Vv(t)=25000t2;v(0.002)=0.100V

  2. Second interval

    Add charge supplied by the 100-mA plateau for 3 ms.

    v(0.005)=0.100+0.100(0.005−0.002)0.001=0.400 Vv(0.005)=0.100+\frac{0.100(0.005-0.002)}{0.001}=0.400\,\mathrm Vv(0.005)=0.100+0.0010.100(0.005−0.002)​=0.400V
Result
v(2 ms)=100 mV,v(5 ms)=400 mVv(2\,\mathrm{ms})=100\,\mathrm{mV},\quad v(5\,\mathrm{ms})=400\,\mathrm{mV}v(2ms)=100mV,v(5ms)=400mV

Check. Triangle area gives 0.1 mC at 2 ms; total area gives 0.4 mC at 5 ms.

Problem

Under DC conditions find energies in the 2-mF and 4-mF capacitors of Fig. 6.12: a 6-mA source feeds a 3-kΩ shunt and a 2-kΩ/4-kΩ series path; the 2-mF capacitor spans 2 kΩ and the 4-mF capacitor is below a 5-kΩ resistor.

    Open both capacitors. The 5-kΩ branch carries no current.

    I2k,4k=633+2+4=2 mAI_{2k,4k}=6\frac{3}{3+2+4}=2\,\mathrm{mA}I2k,4k​=63+2+43​=2mA

  2. Capacitor voltages

    The open branch has no 5-kΩ voltage drop.

    V2mF=2000(0.002)=4 V,V4mF=4000(0.002)=8 VV_{2mF}=2000(0.002)=4\,\mathrm V,\quad V_{4mF}=4000(0.002)=8\,\mathrm VV2mF​=2000(0.002)=4V,V4mF​=4000(0.002)=8V

  3. Stored energies

    Apply w = CV²/2 to each capacitor.

    w1=12(0.002)(4)2=0.016 J;w2=12(0.004)(8)2=0.128 Jw_1=\tfrac12(0.002)(4)^2=0.016\,\mathrm J;\quad w_2=\tfrac12(0.004)(8)^2=0.128\,\mathrm Jw1​=21​(0.002)(4)2=0.016J;w2​=21​(0.004)(8)2=0.128J
Result
w2mF=16 mJ,w4mF=128 mJw_{2mF}=16\,\mathrm{mJ},\quad w_{4mF}=128\,\mathrm{mJ}w2mF​=16mJ,w4mF​=128mJ

Check. The common source-node voltage is 12 V: 4 mA through 3 kΩ plus 2 mA through the other path equals 6 mA.

Problem

Find equivalent capacitance at a–b in Fig. 6.16: 5 μF and the left 20 μF form a series branch, parallel with 6 μF and the right 20 μF; that combination is in series with 60 μF.

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Left series pair

    For two series capacitors use product over sum.

    Ca=20(5)20+5=4 μFC_a=\frac{20(5)}{20+5}=4\,\mu\mathrm FCa​=20+520(5)​=4μF

  2. Parallel group

    Add capacitances sharing both nodes.

    Cb=4+6+20=30 μFC_b=4+6+20=30\,\mu\mathrm FCb​=4+6+20=30μF

  3. Final series pair

    Combine the 30-μF group with 60 μF.

    Ceq=30(60)30+60=20 μFC_{eq}=\frac{30(60)}{30+60}=20\,\mu\mathrm FCeq​=30+6030(60)​=20μF
Result
Ceq=20 μFC_{eq}=20\,\mu\mathrm FCeq​=20μF

Check. The final series equivalent is below both 30 μF and 60 μF.

Problem

View source diagram / question page

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Differentiate current

    Use the product rule.

    didt=10e−5t(1−5t)\frac{di}{dt}=10e^{-5t}(1-5t)dtdi​=10e−5t(1−5t)

  2. Voltage

    Multiply by the inductance.

    v=0.1didt=e−5t(1−5t) Vv=0.1\frac{di}{dt}=e^{-5t}(1-5t)\,\mathrm Vv=0.1dtdi​=e−5t(1−5t)V

  3. Energy

    Square the entire current expression.

    w=12(0.1)(10te−5t)2=5t2e−10t Jw=\tfrac12(0.1)(10te^{-5t})^2=5t^2e^{-10t}\,\mathrm Jw=21​(0.1)(10te−5t)2=5t2e−10tJ
Result
v(t)=(1−5t)e−5t V,w(t)=5t2e−10t Jv(t)=(1-5t)e^{-5t}\,\mathrm V,\quad w(t)=5t^2e^{-10t}\,\mathrm Jv(t)=(1−5t)e−5tV,w(t)=5t2e−10tJ

Check. At t = 0.2 s, current and energy reach their maximum and voltage is zero.

Problem

Under DC conditions in Fig. 6.27 (12-V source, 1-Ω and 5-Ω top resistors, 4-Ω/1-F capacitor branch, and 2-H inductor), find i, vC, iL and stored energies.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. DC equivalent

    Open the capacitor and short the inductor. Only the 1-Ω and 5-Ω series path conducts.

    i=iL=121+5=2 Ai=i_L=\frac{12}{1+5}=2\,\mathrm Ai=iL​=1+512​=2A

  2. Capacitor voltage

    No current flows in 4 Ω, so its drop is zero.

    vC=5i=10 Vv_C=5i=10\,\mathrm VvC​=5i=10V

  3. Energy

    Use the capacitor voltage and inductor current.

    wC=12(1)(10)2=50 J;wL=12(2)(2)2=4 Jw_C=\tfrac12(1)(10)^2=50\,\mathrm J;\quad w_L=\tfrac12(2)(2)^2=4\,\mathrm JwC​=21​(1)(10)2=50J;wL​=21​(2)(2)2=4J
Result
i=iL=2 A, vC=10 V, wC=50 J, wL=4 Ji=i_L=2\,\mathrm A,\ v_C=10\,\mathrm V,\ w_C=50\,\mathrm J,\ w_L=4\,\mathrm Ji=iL​=2A, vC​=10V, wC​=50J, wL​=4J

Check. The resistor drops 2 V and 10 V sum to the 12-V source.

Result

Problem

Problem 6.16: 14 μF is parallel with a series combination of C and 80 μF. The equivalent is 30 μF. Find C.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Required series equivalent

    Subtract the direct parallel capacitor.

    Cs=30−14=16 μFC_s=30-14=16\,\mu\mathrm FCs​=30−14=16μF

  2. Solve the series formula

    Cross-multiply and collect terms.

    80C80+C=16⇒80C=1280+16C⇒C=20 μF\frac{80C}{80+C}=16\Rightarrow80C=1280+16C\Rightarrow C=20\,\mu\mathrm F80+C80C​=16⇒80C=1280+16C⇒C=20μF
Result
C=20 μFC=20\,\mu\mathrm FC=20μF

Check. 14+20(80)/(20+80)=30 μF.

Problem

Problem 6.17: find equivalent capacitance for the three networks in Fig. 6.51, parts (a), (b) and (c). All values are farads.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Part (a)

    The right 12-F/4-F series branch is parallel with 3 F and 6 F, then in series with the input 4 F.

    Cr=12(4)/(12+4)=3;Cp=3+3+6=12;Ca=4(12)/(4+12)=3 FC_r=12(4)/(12+4)=3;\quad C_p=3+3+6=12;\quad C_a=4(12)/(4+12)=3\,\mathrm FCr​=12(4)/(12+4)=3;Cp​=3+3+6=12;Ca​=4(12)/(4+12)=3F

  2. Part (b)

    Combine right 4 F and 2 F in parallel, then series with 6 F, then parallel with 5 F.

    Cb=5+6(4+2)6+4+2=8 FC_b=5+\frac{6(4+2)}{6+4+2}=8\,\mathrm FCb​=5+6+4+26(4+2)​=8F

  3. Part (c)

    The upper 3-F/6-F series pair is parallel with 4 F. Combine that 6-F group in series with outer 2 F and 3 F.

    Cp=3(6)3+6+4=6;Cc=(1/2+1/6+1/3)−1=1 FC_p=\frac{3(6)}{3+6}+4=6;\quad C_c=(1/2+1/6+1/3)^{-1}=1\,\mathrm FCp​=3+63(6)​+4=6;Cc​=(1/2+1/6+1/3)−1=1F
Result
Ca=3 F,Cb=8 F,Cc=1 FC_a=3\,\mathrm F,\quad C_b=8\,\mathrm F,\quad C_c=1\,\mathrm FCa​=3F,Cb​=8F,Cc​=1F

Check. Each final series group is below its smallest series member; part (b) exceeds its 5-F parallel branch.

Problem

Problem 6.18: all eight capacitors in Fig. 6.52 are 4 μF. Find equivalent capacitance between the lower inner terminals.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Top bridge

    The two capacitors between the upper left/right nodes are parallel.

    Ctop=4+4=8 μFC_{top}=4+4=8\,\mu\mathrm FCtop​=4+4=8μF

  2. Each side

    Each side contains a direct 4-μF branch in parallel with a 4-μF/4-μF series path.

    Cside=4+4(4)4+4=6 μFC_{side}=4+\frac{4(4)}{4+4}=6\,\mu\mathrm FCside​=4+4+44(4)​=6μF

  3. Final series chain

    Combine left 6 μF, top 8 μF and right 6 μF.

    Ceq=(16+18+16)−1=2411 μFC_{eq}=\left(\frac16+\frac18+\frac16\right)^{-1}=\frac{24}{11}\,\mu\mathrm FCeq​=(61​+81​+61​)−1=1124​μF
Result
Ceq=2.1818 μFC_{eq}=2.1818\,\mu\mathrm FCeq​=2.1818μF

Check. The equivalent is smaller than each 6-, 8-, and 6-μF series group.

Worked solution · 3 steps

    All three capacitors share 150 V.

    Ceq=5+10+20=35 μFC_{eq}=5+10+20=35\,\mu\mathrm FCeq​=5+10+20=35μF

  2. Individual charges

    Use q = CV for each capacitor.

    q1=5(150)=750 μC;q2=1500 μC;q3=3000 μCq_1=5(150)=750\,\mu\mathrm C;\quad q_2=1500\,\mu\mathrm C;\quad q_3=3000\,\mu\mathrm Cq1​=5(150)=750μC;q2​=1500μC;q3​=3000μC

  3. Total energy

    Use total capacitance with the common voltage.

    w=12(35×10−6)(150)2=0.39375 Jw=\tfrac12(35\times10^{-6})(150)^2=0.39375\,\mathrm Jw=21​(35×10−6)(150)2=0.39375J
Result
Ceq=35 μF; q1=0.75 mC, q2=1.5 mC, q3=3 mC; w=393.75 mJC_{eq}=35\,\mu\mathrm F;\ q_1=0.75\,\mathrm{mC},\ q_2=1.5\,\mathrm{mC},\ q_3=3\,\mathrm{mC};\ w=393.75\,\mathrm{mJ}Ceq​=35μF; q1​=0.75mC, q2​=1.5mC, q3​=3mC; w=393.75mJ

Problem

Problem 6.32: i_s=50e^{-2t} mA flows through a 12-μF capacitor into parallel 20-μF and 40-μF capacitors. Given v₁(0)=50 V and v₂(0)=20 V with shown polarities, find v₁(t), v₂(t), and each capacitor energy at 0.5 s.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 4 steps

  1. Delivered charge

    The same total charge enters the 12-μF capacitor and the 60-μF parallel group.

    Δq=∫0t0.050e−2sds=0.025(1−e−2t) C\Delta q=\int_0^t0.050e^{-2s}ds=0.025(1-e^{-2t})\,\mathrm CΔq=∫0t​0.050e−2sds=0.025(1−e−2t)C

  2. Voltages

    Add Δq/C to the initial voltages.

    v1=50+0.02512×10−6(1−e−2t);v2=20+0.02560×10−6(1−e−2t)v_1=50+\frac{0.025}{12\times10^{-6}}(1-e^{-2t});\quad v_2=20+\frac{0.025}{60\times10^{-6}}(1-e^{-2t})v1​=50+12×10−60.025​(1−e−2t);v2​=20+60×10−60.025​(1−e−2t)

  3. At 0.5 seconds

    Evaluate without prematurely rounding.

    v1=1366.917831 V;v2=283.383566 Vv_1=1366.917831\,\mathrm V;\quad v_2=283.383566\,\mathrm Vv1​=1366.917831V;v2​=283.383566V

  4. Stored energies

    Each parallel capacitor has v₂; the 12-μF capacitor has v₁.

    w12=12(12×10−6)v12=11.210786 J;w20=0.803062 J;w40=1.606125 Jw_{12}=\tfrac12(12\times10^{-6})v_1^2=11.210786\,\mathrm J;\quad w_{20}=0.803062\,\mathrm J;\quad w_{40}=1.606125\,\mathrm Jw12​=21​(12×10−6)v12​=11.210786J;w20​=0.803062J;w40​=1.606125J
Result
v1=50+2083.333333(1−e−2t) V;v2=20+416.666667(1−e−2t) V;(w12,w20,w40)=(11.210786,0.803062,1.606125) Jv_1=50+2083.333333(1-e^{-2t})\,\mathrm V;\quad v_2=20+416.666667(1-e^{-2t})\,\mathrm V;\quad (w_{12},w_{20},w_{40})=(11.210786,0.803062,1.606125)\,\mathrm Jv1​=50+2083.333333(1−e−2t)V;v2​=20+416.666667(1−e−2t)V;(w12​,w20​,w40​)=(11.210786,0.803062,1.606125)J

Check. C₁dv₁/dt and (C₂+C₃)dv₂/dt both reproduce 50e^{-2t} mA. Released key rounds intermediate coefficients, giving slightly different energies.

Problem

Problem 6.43: current in an 80-mH inductor rises from zero to 60 mA. Find stored energy.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Convert to SI

    Use L = 0.080 H and I = 0.060 A.

    w=12LI2w=\tfrac12LI^2w=21​LI2

  2. Evaluate

    The initial energy is zero.

    w=12(0.080)(0.060)2=0.000144 Jw=\tfrac12(0.080)(0.060)^2=0.000144\,\mathrm Jw=21​(0.080)(0.060)2=0.000144J
Result
w=144 μJw=144\,\mu\mathrm Jw=144μJ

Check. Energy scales with current squared and is nonnegative.

Problem

Problem 6.51: determine equivalent inductance in Fig. 6.73: a 10-mH direct branch parallels a 25-mH inductor in series with parallel 60-, 20- and 30-mH inductors.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Inner parallel group

    Add reciprocals of uncoupled parallel inductances.

    Lp=(1/60+1/20+1/30)−1=10 mHL_p=(1/60+1/20+1/30)^{-1}=10\,\mathrm{mH}Lp​=(1/60+1/20+1/30)−1=10mH

  2. Series branch

    Add 25 mH to the inner equivalent.

    Ls=25+10=35 mHL_s=25+10=35\,\mathrm{mH}Ls​=25+10=35mH

  3. Final parallel

    Combine 10 mH and 35 mH.

    Leq=10(35)10+35=709 mHL_{eq}=\frac{10(35)}{10+35}=\frac{70}{9}\,\mathrm{mH}Leq​=10+3510(35)​=970​mH
Result
Leq=7.7778 mHL_{eq}=7.7778\,\mathrm{mH}Leq​=7.7778mH

Check. The final parallel equivalent is smaller than 10 mH.

Problem

Problem 6.53: find terminal inductance in Fig. 6.75, with outer series 6 and 10 mH, a direct inner 8-mH vertical branch and the right-hand triangular network shown.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Upper right group

    The upper 8 mH + 12 mH path parallels the diagonal 5 mH.

    Lu=(8+12)∥5=20∥5=4 mHL_u=(8+12)\parallel5=20\parallel5=4\,\mathrm{mH}Lu​=(8+12)∥5=20∥5=4mH

  2. Lower right group

    The lower 8 mH + 4 mH path parallels the diagonal 6 mH.

    Ld=(8+4)∥6=12∥6=4 mHL_d=(8+4)\parallel6=12\parallel6=4\,\mathrm{mH}Ld​=(8+4)∥6=12∥6=4mH

  3. Inner and outer combination

    The two right groups are series, parallel with the inner 8 mH; outer 6 and 10 mH remain series.

    Leq=6+[8∥(4+4)]+10=6+4+10=20 mHL_{eq}=6+[8\parallel(4+4)]+10=6+4+10=20\,\mathrm{mH}Leq​=6+[8∥(4+4)]+10=6+4+10=20mH
Result
Leq=20 mHL_{eq}=20\,\mathrm{mH}Leq​=20mH

Check. Both right-hand reductions equal 4 mH; two equal 8-mH inner paths yield 4 mH.

Problem

Problem 6.60: a 4e^{-2t}-A source feeds parallel 3-H and 5-H inductors. Given downward current i₀(0)=2 A in 5 H, find i₀(t) and common voltage v₀(t) for t>0.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Equivalent inductance

    The common voltage is equivalent inductance times derivative of total current.

    Leq=3∥5=158 H;v0=158ddt(4e−2t)=−15e−2t VL_{eq}=3\parallel5=\frac{15}{8}\,\mathrm H;\quad v_0=\frac{15}{8}\frac{d}{dt}(4e^{-2t})=-15e^{-2t}\,\mathrm VLeq​=3∥5=815​H;v0​=815​dtd​(4e−2t)=−15e−2tV

  2. Integrate branch current

    Use the 5-H branch initial condition.

    i0(t)=2+15∫0t−15e−2sds=0.5+1.5e−2t Ai_0(t)=2+\frac15\int_0^t-15e^{-2s}ds=0.5+1.5e^{-2t}\,\mathrm Ai0​(t)=2+51​∫0t​−15e−2sds=0.5+1.5e−2tA
Result
i0(t)=0.5+1.5e−2t A;v0(t)=−15e−2t Vi_0(t)=0.5+1.5e^{-2t}\,\mathrm A;\quad v_0(t)=-15e^{-2t}\,\mathrm Vi0​(t)=0.5+1.5e−2tA;v0​(t)=−15e−2tV

Check. i₀(0)=2 A and 5 di₀/dt=v₀. At long time the ideal parallel inductors retain equal and opposite circulating currents.

Problem

For Fig. 7.5, vC(0)=15 V, C=0.1 F, and the capacitor sees a 5-Ω branch in parallel with an 8-Ω/12-Ω series branch. Find vC, vx across 12 Ω, and downward ix for t>0.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Equivalent resistance

    Combine the two discharge paths.

    Req=5∥(8+12)=4 Ω;τ=4(0.1)=0.4 sR_{eq}=5\parallel(8+12)=4\,\Omega;\quad\tau=4(0.1)=0.4\,\mathrm sReq​=5∥(8+12)=4Ω;τ=4(0.1)=0.4s

  2. Capacitor discharge

    Use the initial voltage.

    vC=15e−t/0.4=15e−2.5t Vv_C=15e^{-t/0.4}=15e^{-2.5t}\,\mathrm VvC​=15e−t/0.4=15e−2.5tV

  3. Output branch

    Divide voltage across the series path and use Ohm’s law.

    vx=1220vC=9e−2.5t V;ix=vC20=0.75e−2.5t Av_x=\frac{12}{20}v_C=9e^{-2.5t}\,\mathrm V;\quad i_x=\frac{v_C}{20}=0.75e^{-2.5t}\,\mathrm Avx​=2012​vC​=9e−2.5tV;ix​=20vC​​=0.75e−2.5tA
Result
vC=15e−2.5t V,vx=9e−2.5t V,ix=0.75e−2.5t Av_C=15e^{-2.5t}\,\mathrm V,\quad v_x=9e^{-2.5t}\,\mathrm V,\quad i_x=0.75e^{-2.5t}\,\mathrm AvC​=15e−2.5tV,vx​=9e−2.5tV,ix​=0.75e−2.5tA

Check. At t = 0, resistor currents total 15/5+15/20 = 3.75 A, equal to −C dvC/dt.

Problem

The switch in Fig. 7.8 opens after a long time. The 20-V source initially feeds 3 Ω then a 9-Ω shunt and a 1-Ω/20-mF capacitor branch. Find v(t) and initial capacitor energy.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Initial voltage

    At DC the capacitor is open, so no current flows in 1 Ω.

    v(0−)=2093+9=15 V=v(0+)v(0^-)=20\frac9{3+9}=15\,\mathrm V=v(0^+)v(0−)=203+99​=15V=v(0+)

  2. After opening

    The source disconnects; 1 Ω and 9 Ω are in series across the capacitor.

    Req=10 Ω;τ=10(0.020)=0.2 sR_{eq}=10\,\Omega;\quad\tau=10(0.020)=0.2\,\mathrm sReq​=10Ω;τ=10(0.020)=0.2s

  3. Voltage and energy

    Apply the natural response and energy formula.

    v(t)=15e−5t V;w(0)=12(0.020)(15)2=2.25 Jv(t)=15e^{-5t}\,\mathrm V;\quad w(0)=\tfrac12(0.020)(15)^2=2.25\,\mathrm Jv(t)=15e−5tV;w(0)=21​(0.020)(15)2=2.25J
Result
v(t)=15e−5t V,w(0)=2.25 Jv(t)=15e^{-5t}\,\mathrm V,\quad w(0)=2.25\,\mathrm Jv(t)=15e−5tV,w(0)=2.25J

Check. Voltage starts continuously at 15 V and tends to zero.

Problem

The switch in Fig. 7.16 opens after a long time. Find downward current in the 2-H inductor: source 40 V, initial 2-Ω series resistor, 12-Ω shunt, 4-Ω top resistor and 16-Ω shunt parallel with the inductor.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 4 steps

  1. Initial DC circuit

    Short the inductor; it bypasses 16 Ω.

    Rin=2+(12∥4)=5 Ω;Is=40/5=8 AR_{in}=2+(12\parallel4)=5\,\Omega;\quad I_s=40/5=8\,\mathrm ARin​=2+(12∥4)=5Ω;Is​=40/5=8A

  2. Initial inductor current

    The parallel section has 40−2(8)=24 V.

    i(0−)=24/4=6 A=i(0+)i(0^-)=24/4=6\,\mathrm A=i(0^+)i(0−)=24/4=6A=i(0+)

  3. Discharge resistance

    After opening, the inductor sees 16 Ω in parallel with 4 Ω + 12 Ω.

    Req=16∥16=8 Ω;τ=L/R=2/8=0.25 sR_{eq}=16\parallel16=8\,\Omega;\quad\tau=L/R=2/8=0.25\,\mathrm sReq​=16∥16=8Ω;τ=L/R=2/8=0.25s

  4. Natural response

    Insert initial current and time constant.

    i(t)=6e−t/0.25=6e−4t Ai(t)=6e^{-t/0.25}=6e^{-4t}\,\mathrm Ai(t)=6e−t/0.25=6e−4tA
Result
i(t)=6e−4t A(t>0)i(t)=6e^{-4t}\,\mathrm A\quad(t>0)i(t)=6e−4tA(t>0)

Check. L di/dt = −48e^{-4t} V and −R_eq i gives the same voltage.

Problem

A 0.5-mF capacitor has been connected to position A (24-V source, 3-kΩ/5-kΩ divider). At t=0 it moves to B, a 30-V source through 4 kΩ. Find v(t), v(1 s), v(4 s).

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Initial voltage

    The DC divider sets the initial voltage.

    v(0)=2453+5=15 Vv(0)=24\frac5{3+5}=15\,\mathrm Vv(0)=243+55​=15V

  2. Final state and time constant

    At B the final voltage is 30 V and resistance is 4 kΩ.

    τ=4000(0.0005)=2 s\tau=4000(0.0005)=2\,\mathrm sτ=4000(0.0005)=2s

  3. Complete response

    Use final + (initial − final) exp(−t/τ).

    v(t)=30−15e−t/2 V;v(1)=20.902 V;v(4)=27.970 Vv(t)=30-15e^{-t/2}\,\mathrm V;\quad v(1)=20.902\,\mathrm V;\quad v(4)=27.970\,\mathrm Vv(t)=30−15e−t/2V;v(1)=20.902V;v(4)=27.970V
Result
v(t)=30−15e−t/2 V; v(1)=20.90 V; v(4)=27.97 Vv(t)=30-15e^{-t/2}\,\mathrm V;\ v(1)=20.90\,\mathrm V;\ v(4)=27.97\,\mathrm Vv(t)=30−15e−t/2V; v(1)=20.90V; v(4)=27.97V

Check. The response rises continuously from 15 V toward 30 V.

Problem

In Fig. 7.45 the switch opens at t=0 after a long time. A 30u(t)-V source feeds 10 Ω into a 20-Ω shunt and 1/4-F capacitor; a switched 10-V source initially fixes the capacitor voltage. Find v and source-resistor current i for all time.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Before switching

    The 30u(t) source is zero; the 10-V source fixes capacitor voltage.

    v(t)=10 V;i(t)=0−1010=−1 A(t<0)v(t)=10\,\mathrm V;\quad i(t)=\frac{0-10}{10}=-1\,\mathrm A\quad(t<0)v(t)=10V;i(t)=100−10​=−1A(t<0)

  2. Final voltage and time constant

    After opening the divider is driven by 30 V.

    v(∞)=302010+20=20 V;τ=(10∥20)14=53 sv(\infty)=30\frac{20}{10+20}=20\,\mathrm V;\quad\tau=(10\parallel20)\frac14=\frac53\,\mathrm sv(∞)=3010+2020​=20V;τ=(10∥20)41​=35​s

  3. After switching

    Voltage is continuous, but resistor current may jump.

    v(t)=20−10e−0.6t V;i(t)=30−v(t)10=1+e−0.6t A(t>0)v(t)=20-10e^{-0.6t}\,\mathrm V;\quad i(t)=\frac{30-v(t)}{10}=1+e^{-0.6t}\,\mathrm A\quad(t>0)v(t)=20−10e−0.6tV;i(t)=1030−v(t)​=1+e−0.6tA(t>0)
Result
v={10t<020−10e−0.6tt>0V;i={−1t<01+e−0.6tt>0Av=\begin{cases}10&t<0\\20-10e^{-0.6t}&t>0\end{cases}\mathrm V;\quad i=\begin{cases}-1&t<0\\1+e^{-0.6t}&t>0\end{cases}\mathrm Av={1020−10e−0.6t​t<0t>0​V;i={−11+e−0.6t​t<0t>0​A

Check. v(0−)=v(0+)=10 V. Current jumps from −1 A to 2 A because the source and switch change.

Problem

A 10-V source feeds 2 Ω, then a 3-Ω resistor bypassed by a switch, then a 1/3-H inductor. The switch opens at t=0 after being closed a long time. Find i(t) for t>0.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Initial current

    The closed switch bypasses 3 Ω; the DC inductor is a short.

    i(0−)=10/2=5 A=i(0+)i(0^-)=10/2=5\,\mathrm A=i(0^+)i(0−)=10/2=5A=i(0+)

  2. Final current and time constant

    After opening both resistors carry the inductor current.

    i(∞)=10/(2+3)=2 A;τ=1/35=115 si(\infty)=10/(2+3)=2\,\mathrm A;\quad\tau=\frac{1/3}{5}=\frac1{15}\,\mathrm si(∞)=10/(2+3)=2A;τ=51/3​=151​s

  3. Complete response

    Insert initial and final values.

    i(t)=2+(5−2)e−15t Ai(t)=2+(5-2)e^{-15t}\,\mathrm Ai(t)=2+(5−2)e−15tA
Result
i(t)=2+3e−15t Ai(t)=2+3e^{-15t}\,\mathrm Ai(t)=2+3e−15tA

Check. The differential equation (1/3)di/dt+5i=10 holds for all t>0.

Result
v(t)=6.666667e−12.5t Vv(t)=6.666667e^{-12.5t}\,\mathrm Vv(t)=6.666667e−12.5tV

    Short the inductor. The shunt equivalent is 4||8=8/3 Ω.

  2. After opening

    The inductor discharges through the 4-Ω and 8-Ω series path.

    Req=12 Ω;τ=4/12=1/3 sR_{eq}=12\,\Omega;\quad\tau=4/12=1/3\,\mathrm sReq​=12Ω;τ=4/12=1/3s

  3. Natural response

    Inductor current is continuous.

    i0(t)=1.2e−3t Ai_0(t)=1.2e^{-3t}\,\mathrm Ai0​(t)=1.2e−3tA
Result
i0(t)=1.2e−3t Ai_0(t)=1.2e^{-3t}\,\mathrm Ai0​(t)=1.2e−3tA

Problem

Problem 7.13: in a source-free RL loop v(t)=80e^{-1000t} V and i(t)=5e^{-1000t} mA. Current leaves the inductor’s marked positive terminal. Find R, L, τ and resistor energy over 0<t<0.5 ms.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Resistance and time constant

    The resistor receives the shown voltage and current. The exponent gives 1/τ.

    R=800.005=16000 Ω;τ=1/1000=1 msR=\frac{80}{0.005}=16000\,\Omega;\quad\tau=1/1000=1\,\mathrm{ms}R=0.00580​=16000Ω;τ=1/1000=1ms

  2. Inductance

    Use L = Rτ. The non-passive reference on the inductor gives v = −L di/dt.

    L=16000(0.001)=16 HL=16000(0.001)=16\,\mathrm HL=16000(0.001)=16H

  3. Dissipated energy

    Integrate positive resistor power.

    p=vi=0.4e−2000t W;W=∫00.00050.4e−2000tdt=0.0002(1−e−1) Jp=vi=0.4e^{-2000t}\,\mathrm W;\quad W=\int_0^{0.0005}0.4e^{-2000t}dt=0.0002(1-e^{-1})\,\mathrm Jp=vi=0.4e−2000tW;W=∫00.0005​0.4e−2000tdt=0.0002(1−e−1)J
Result
R=16 kΩ, L=16 H, τ=1 ms, WR=126.424 μJR=16\,\mathrm{k}\Omega,\ L=16\,\mathrm H,\ \tau=1\,\mathrm{ms},\ W_R=126.424\,\mu\mathrm JR=16kΩ, L=16H, τ=1ms, WR​=126.424μJ

Check. Initial magnetic energy is 200 μJ; subtracting its remaining value 200e^{-1} μJ gives the same dissipation.

Problem

Problem 7.14: find the time constant of a 5-mH inductor with two parallel discharge paths: 20 kΩ + 40 kΩ and 10 kΩ + 30 kΩ.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Equivalent resistance

    Each side is a series path; the two paths are parallel.

    Req=60∥40=24 kΩR_{eq}=60\parallel40=24\,\mathrm{k}\OmegaReq​=60∥40=24kΩ

  2. Time constant

    Use L/R with henries and ohms.

    τ=0.00524000=2.08333×10−7 s\tau=\frac{0.005}{24000}=2.08333\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm sτ=240000.005​=2.08333×10−7s
Result
τ=0.208333 μs\tau=0.208333\,\mu\mathrm sτ=0.208333μs

Check. A small inductance and large discharge resistance give a very short time constant.

Problem

Problem 7.39: find capacitor voltage before and after switching for both Fig. 7.106 circuits. (a) 20 V, series 4 Ω, C=2 F, switched 1-Ω shunt opens. (b) 12-V/3-Ω branch, C=2 F with left-positive voltage, and right 4-Ω/2-A parallel branch becomes shorted.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 4 steps

  1. Part (a), initial and final

    Before opening the 1-Ω branch forms a divider; afterwards the capacitor approaches 20 V.

    va(0)=2014+1=4 V;va(∞)=20 Vv_a(0)=20\frac1{4+1}=4\,\mathrm V;\quad v_a(\infty)=20\,\mathrm Vva​(0)=204+11​=4V;va​(∞)=20V

  2. Part (a), response

    The remaining resistance is 4 Ω.

    τa=4(2)=8 s;va(t)=20−16e−t/8 V(t>0)\tau_a=4(2)=8\,\mathrm s;\quad v_a(t)=20-16e^{-t/8}\,\mathrm V\quad(t>0)τa​=4(2)=8s;va​(t)=20−16e−t/8V(t>0)

  3. Part (b), initial and final

    Initially the left capacitor plate is at 12 V and the right plate at 2×4=8 V relative to the lower node. Closing the switch makes the right plate zero.

    vb(0)=12−8=4 V;vb(∞)=12 Vv_b(0)=12-8=4\,\mathrm V;\quad v_b(\infty)=12\,\mathrm Vvb​(0)=12−8=4V;vb​(∞)=12V

  4. Part (b), response

    After closing, only 3 Ω determines the capacitor time constant.

    τb=3(2)=6 s;vb(t)=12−8e−t/6 V(t>0)\tau_b=3(2)=6\,\mathrm s;\quad v_b(t)=12-8e^{-t/6}\,\mathrm V\quad(t>0)τb​=3(2)=6s;vb​(t)=12−8e−t/6V(t>0)
Result
va={4t<020−16e−t/8t>0V;vb={4t<012−8e−t/6t>0Vv_a=\begin{cases}4&t<0\\20-16e^{-t/8}&t>0\end{cases}\mathrm V;\quad v_b=\begin{cases}4&t<0\\12-8e^{-t/6}&t>0\end{cases}\mathrm Vva​={420−16e−t/8​t<0t>0​V;vb​={412−8e−t/6​t<0t>0​V

Check. Both capacitor voltages remain 4 V at switching and approach their new DC values.

Problem

Problem 7.40: find capacitor voltage before and after switching. (a) A 3-F capacitor changes from a 12-V source through 3 Ω + 2 Ω to a 4-V source through 2 Ω. (b) A 6-A source parallels 2 Ω, feeds a 5-F capacitor through 4 Ω, and a switch bypasses the 4-Ω resistor at t=0.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 4 steps

  1. Part (a), boundary values

    At DC neither resistor has a drop; switching changes the final voltage from 12 V to 4 V.

    va(0)=12 V;va(∞)=4 V;τa=2(3)=6 sv_a(0)=12\,\mathrm V;\quad v_a(\infty)=4\,\mathrm V;\quad\tau_a=2(3)=6\,\mathrm sva​(0)=12V;va​(∞)=4V;τa​=2(3)=6s

  2. Part (a), response

    Use the complete RC response.

    va(t)=4+8e−t/6 V(t>0)v_a(t)=4+8e^{-t/6}\,\mathrm V\quad(t>0)va​(t)=4+8e−t/6V(t>0)

  3. Part (b), no transient amplitude

    The capacitor is open at DC, so no current flows through 4 Ω initially. The source sets 6×2=12 V before and after switching.

    vb(0)=vb(∞)=12 V;τafter=2(5)=10 sv_b(0)=v_b(\infty)=12\,\mathrm V;\quad\tau_{after}=2(5)=10\,\mathrm svb​(0)=vb​(∞)=12V;τafter​=2(5)=10s

  4. Part (b), constant voltage

    The exponential coefficient is zero.

    vb(t)=12+(12−12)e−t/10=12 Vv_b(t)=12+(12-12)e^{-t/10}=12\,\mathrm Vvb​(t)=12+(12−12)e−t/10=12V
Result
va={12t<04+8e−t/6t>0V;vb=12 V for all tv_a=\begin{cases}12&t<0\\4+8e^{-t/6}&t>0\end{cases}\mathrm V;\quad v_b=12\,\mathrm V\ \text{for all }tva​={124+8e−t/6​t<0t>0​V;vb​=12V for all t

Check. Switching a resistance need not create a transient when the initial and final capacitor voltages coincide.

Problem

Problem 7.42: Fig. 7.109 has a 12-V source and 2-Ω series resistor connected by a switch to parallel 4-Ω and 3-F branches. Find v₀(t) for (a) closing after a long open interval and (b) opening after a long closed interval.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Part (a), initial and final

    Initially the capacitor has discharged through 4 Ω. After closing the divider sets its final voltage.

    v0(0)=0;v0(∞)=1242+4=8 Vv_0(0)=0;\quad v_0(\infty)=12\frac4{2+4}=8\,\mathrm Vv0​(0)=0;v0​(∞)=122+44​=8V

  2. Part (a), charging response

    Deactivate the source to find 2||4 Ω.

    τa=(2∥4)(3)=4 s;v0a(t)=8(1−e−t/4) V\tau_a=(2\parallel4)(3)=4\,\mathrm s;\quad v_{0a}(t)=8(1-e^{-t/4})\,\mathrm Vτa​=(2∥4)(3)=4s;v0a​(t)=8(1−e−t/4)V

  3. Part (b), discharge response

    Start at 8 V. Opening disconnects the 2-Ω source branch; discharge occurs through 4 Ω.

    τb=4(3)=12 s;v0b(t)=8e−t/12 V\tau_b=4(3)=12\,\mathrm s;\quad v_{0b}(t)=8e^{-t/12}\,\mathrm Vτb​=4(3)=12s;v0b​(t)=8e−t/12V
Result
(a) v0(t)=8(1−e−t/4) V;(b) v0(t)=8e−t/12 V(t>0)\text{(a) }v_0(t)=8(1-e^{-t/4})\,\mathrm V;\qquad\text{(b) }v_0(t)=8e^{-t/12}\,\mathrm V\quad(t>0)(a) v0​(t)=8(1−e−t/4)V;(b) v0​(t)=8e−t/12V(t>0)

Check. Closing uses the parallel resistance 2||4 Ω; opening uses 4 Ω alone, so discharge is three times slower.

Problem

The switch has been closed a long time and opens at t = 0. Find i(0+), v(0+), their initial derivatives, and the final values.

View source diagram / question page

Original page for topology, polarities, and reference directions. Some lecture and key pages also show answers. Open the original file for full resolution.

Worked solution · 4 steps

  1. Before switching: DC equivalents

    Short the inductor and open the capacitor. The 4 Ω and 2 Ω resistors carry the same current.

    i(0−)=124+2=2 A,v(0−)=2(2)=4 Vi(0^-)=\frac{12}{4+2}=2\ \mathrm A,\quad v(0^-)=2(2)=4\ \mathrm Vi(0−)=4+212​=2 A,v(0−)=2(2)=4 V

  2. Carry the stored values across the switch

    Inductor current and capacitor voltage remain continuous.

    i(0+)=2 A,v(0+)=4 Vi(0^+)=2\ \mathrm A,\quad v(0^+)=4\ \mathrm Vi(0+)=2 A,v(0+)=4 V

  3. Use the circuit after switching

    The 2 Ω branch is disconnected. Apply KVL and the capacitor equation.

    i′(0+)=12−4(2)−40.25=0,v′(0+)=20.1=20 V/si'(0^+)=\frac{12-4(2)-4}{0.25}=0,\quad v'(0^+)=\frac2{0.1}=20\ \mathrm{V/s}i′(0+)=0.2512−4(2)−4​=0,v′(0+)=0.12​=20 V/s

  4. Let the circuit reach DC again

    The capacitor becomes open, so no current flows through the series resistor.

    i(∞)=0,v(∞)=12 Vi(\infty)=0,\quad v(\infty)=12\ \mathrm Vi(∞)=0,v(∞)=12 V
Result
i0=2 A, v0=4 V, i0′=0, v0′=20 V/si_0=2\ \mathrm A,\ v_0=4\ \mathrm V,\ i'_0=0,\ v'_0=20\ \mathrm{V/s}i0​=2 A, v0​=4 V, i0′​=0, v0′​=20 V/s

Check. The final capacitor voltage equals the supply; the final series current is zero.
